utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to everyone. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor against Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is the 11th of July, Tuesday, 2006. I'd like to say good morning to all those in the courtroom. This is our last sitting before the recess in which -- and we continue in August. I was told that the witness is running late and will be here in about ten minutes. It is a traffic problem and a technical difficulty, so we've got a few minutes before he arrives. Not to waste time, let us deal with the exhibits straight away for the previous witness, Manolic. That was placed on standby, that matter, and I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Scott and then we'll hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Yes, Your Honours, the Prosecution would tender -- or does tender the following exhibits concerning the witness Manolic: 37 -- sorry, I should say P 00037, P 00068, P 00134, P 00312, P 00699, P 01325, P 01452, P 01883, P 02122, P 02302, P 03704, P 03112, P 04740, P 05498, P 06123, P 08012, P 09645, P 09649, and P 09673, which is the Manolic book, and specifically the following pages: 210, 246 to 250, 262 to 267, 281 to 288, 317 to 327. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence. I know that it was Mr. Praljak's Defence and Mr. Prlic's Defence, as well as Stojic and Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Coric as well. Now, the numbers -- Mr. Karnavas, would you like to start off?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. If I could start first by responding to the Prosecution's offer. Given that we are in an adversarial setting and given the nature of the proceedings here, we both -- we can't have it both ways where the Prosecution just introduces documents and the Defence is limited in time of cross-examination. It's our collective position, as I understand it, that only documents that are presented to the witness for the witness to comment on should be introduced, particularly if they're presidential transcripts. If the witness isn't given an opportunity to comment on it, I don't believe that simply -- it should just come in simply because it was shown to the particular witness without any particular comment. With respect to the book, I believe the entire book should be translated, not just snippets of it, so I -- we don't have an objection to that book coming in, but it should be the entire book and not just part of it. As far as documents from the Prlic Defence team, on page 4613 I misspoke apparently. I introduced a document as 1D 270012. The correct number should be 1D 00526. So that's the document that we are tendering: 1D 00526. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I stressed last time or, rather, I raised an objection last time in line with what Mr. Karnavas said that, respecting the general principle of exhibits, on the list proposed by Mr. Scott we have nine documents which weren't presented to the witness at all, and I said last time that those documents could perhaps be marked for identification but nothing more than that. And Mr. Scott said last time that there will most probably a witness in the future to whom those documents can be shown. So I join in my colleagues to say that I don't think those documents can be admitted into evidence as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We would like to propose 2D 0040 document, and I'd like to join my other colleagues with respect to the transcript. I agree with what Mr. Karnavas said, and I'd like to stress that during the cross-examination we were opposed to the introduction of 01325. That was the transcript from a session which Mr. Manolic himself said he had not attended. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wholly support the standpoints put forward by my colleagues Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Ibrisimovic. That is my own position. I don't wish to repeat it. The only thing that my colleagues omitted to say is this: That the book by Witness Manolic does not have an integral -- is not translated in its entirety, and so they are seeking to have just certain pages admitted into evidence. I think that the book as a whole should be admitted, of course translated in its entirety. And similarly, all the presidential transcripts which are admitted into evidence require an integral translation, not just translations of the excerpts put to the witness. Some of them are already translated, but not all. Now, as far as the Defence of General Praljak is concerned, we would like to propose the following exhibits: Document 3D 0007, 3D 0009, 3D 00010, and 3D 00011, 3D 00142, 3D 00145, 3D 00186, 3D 00295, 3D 00302, 3D 00305, 3D 00306, 3D 00307, 3D 00313, 3D 00314, 3D 00318, 3D 00319, and the last document is the book, 3D 00320. The title is "The Truth About Bosnia-Herzegovina, Documents 1991 to 1995," just the chapters 1 to 5 on pages 53 to 570, and those chapters are systematically listed agreements during the critical period between the involved parties with any comments. Just the agreements. And finally, we used a document that has already been tendered. It is 3D 00006. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good morning. I would like to oppose the proposal made by the Prosecutor that the book by Witness Josip Manolic be tendered into evidence, which is under 09673 P, and if I might be allowed to explain. It is rather lengthy, but I hope it will be useful to the Trial Chamber when it decides on the exhibit. First of all, the book has not been translated in its entirety so the readers, in reading certain pages of the book which have been translated, are still unclear and do not know that Josip Manolic in that book is said to be the author of the syntagma that is used about the historical and natural borders of Croatia which is one of the syntagmas which we are discussing in this trial. Second, the readers, when reading parts of the book that have been translated by the Prosecutor, cannot know that the -- the book was written for the political promotion of Josip Manolic, which is clearly stated on page 14 of the book. Just these two examples can indicate or, rather, show the unreliability of that exhibit. What I consider to be more important, however, is the following: For Witness Manolic to be able to achieve his own political promotion through this book, he incorrectly wrote down the contents of his interviews by changing certain words and sentences and leaving out essential portions of the answers, which makes the interviews in the book have a different meaning. They do not have the meaning in the book that they did at the time they were published because they are not the original integral interviews. The Court will be aware of the fact that the Defence did not have enough time to amass all the original interviews and compare them all with the interviews shown in the book, shown partially in the book, because we received the book as an exhibit just on Friday before the start of the witness's testimony. That is why I just have several objections and comments to make and I'm going to prove what I said so far on the basis of four interviews. The first interview --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker kindly slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- was published in Globus on the 18th of June, 1993, and I'm going briefly to state now, with your permission, what are the key points of the interview that have been left out in the book by Josip Manolic, and I have here the original interviews as well so that I can prove what I'm saying straight away. On page 250 of the book, which is page 3 of the translation of the book, in the first section, the question -- this following question has been left out, and I quote: "Is the information correct that Zagreb is striving for replacing Mate Boban?" And Josip Manolic answered, and I quote: "Zagreb can do as much as striving for changing the policy which led to the above consequences to the Croatian people." So in that interview, Witness Manolic did not strive to have Mate Boban replaced, says something else today. In that same excerpt, the second sentence has been left out from the original -- in the original answer, in the answer in the original interview, and that sentence reads as follows: "Will politics yield to war or war to politics? That's not the main question here for us." The second example from the same interview: Immediately after the answer, we have a question and answer that have been left out of the book, and the question reads as follows: "Does not Boban get political instructions from the cabinet and offices of Zagreb politicians who were born in Herzegovina?" The answer reads as follows: "You'd have to ask them that. You'd have to ask them how much influence they wielded on politics which led us into an open conflict with the Muslims. I cannot assess how great their influence was because over the past year I was not involved in resolving the crisis in BH." The third example from the same interview reads as follows: The last section of the interview is in fact part of a sentence in response to the question: "Does not Croatian policy in BH is reflected between the conflicts within the HDZ and is not the policy in Bosnia the main point of dissent or divergence?" And an answer to that, given by Manolic, is as follows: "I don't think that is the main reason. The main reasons are internal problems, although --" and here we get to the part of the sentence which was published in the book as an integral answer. So today Witness Manolic says that Bosnia was the main point of divergence. In June, 1993, in the original interview which is -- he claims differently, in this falsified version. The second interview from Globus, dated the 10th of September, 1993, which is 2 -- page 262 of the book or, rather, the first page of the translation of that portion of the book, Witness Manolic omitted the last sentence of the original interview, and it reads as follows. I quote: "The set-up of Herceg-Bosna must not --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker repeat what she just said. Could the speaker kindly repeat the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. I'm sorry. The last sentence of the interview, which was left out in the book, it was not published in the book, reads as follows, and I quote: "The set-up in Herceg-Bosna must not be an obstacle to cooperation because the results of the Croatian population throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina leads us along that course." Now, the third interview is one that was published in Danas on the 12th of October, 1993, which is page 263 and 264 of the book or, rather, in the English text it is page 1 and 2 of the translation of that part of the book. Comparing it with the original interview, six vital statements have been left out. Here is the first one, a statement which reads, and I quote: "I do not know up until now any bargain struck between Milosevic and Tudjman thus far, or pact." Second, the beginning of the answer to the question has been left out of why he is criticising Mate Boban, and that part of the answer reads as follows: "I don't think this is the right moment to speak about what I criticise Boban for." Third, the question and answer were left out which, in the original interview, after a statement about how to solve the problem of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that question and answer read as follows, and I quote: "Would that mean abolishing the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna as it now stands?" And the answer is, and I quote: "Would the abolishment of the Croatian Republic -- whether it is abolished or not is -- what is important for us is that national interests of all the ethnic groups be respected living in the territory of that state." I'd just like to say why I consider this to be important. It is because it is clear that after the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Witness Manolic did not consider it to be important whether we -- it was a republic or whether it was some other sort of territorial set-up for Herceg-Bosna. Furthermore, as the fourth example of incorrectly quoted interviews from an answer contained in the third chapter on page 263 of the book, the following sentence was left out, and I quote: "Whether it's going to be a republic or whether it's going to take some other shape for an autonomy is a matter of agreement." Now, the fifth example. The first next question and answer were left out of the book, and the question read as follows: "Are there any differences between you and the Defence Minister, Gojko Susak, with respect to resolving the BH problem?" Witness Manolic answered at the time, and I quote: "I don't know what Gojko Susak advocates, what position he takes. So far he has not made his thoughts clear with the exception of his statement made in the Croatian Sabor parliament and some statements made in Herzegovina." The sixth example. The last section was left out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many more examples do you have, Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a short example from the Globus newspaper, and then a concluding part relating to author's copyright. So the last section of the interview was left out, and it reads as follows, and I quote: "The agreement between Tudjman and Izetbegovic leaves great scope for manoeuvering to Croatian policy on an international level. It strengthens our positions with our neighbours. That is yet further proof of our peaceful policy which we have advocated since the very start of the aggression with our sovereignty." Now I'm going to give an example of the fourth interview or, rather, not, because they are similar. Now, my objections to the book itself: There -- we're not challenging the fact that, according to Croatian law and laws of other countries, interviews are one form in which journalists can express themselves and that copyright over these interviews are held by the journalist not by the individual granting the interview. Without agreement from the journalist, nobody has the right to publish authorised texts of or, rather, texts of journalists without agreement from the author, nor do they have the right to change them in any way, to change a journalist's original -- the author's original work. This would be distortion, and according to Croatian criminal law, it is subject to criminal responsibility and accountability. I tried to ascertain whether Witness Manolic did have agreement from the author of the interviews for publishing those interviews and for distorting the contents of those interviews and I have not succeeded in receiving information or, rather, no journalist has told me that that agreement was indeed given. Therefore, I propose that these exhibits -- this exhibit, on the basis of Rule 89(B) and (D), should not be admitted into evidence because we are not dealing with reliable documents but, rather, they are documents that don't have the necessary probative value. Now, as far as exhibits are concerned for the Defence, we just had one exhibit, and that is why I would like to ask that it be admitted into evidence now. It is 4D 00066. Thank you. And I apologise for taking up so much time but I considered these matters to be very relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we agree with everything that our colleagues have said before us, and we'd like to tender the following exhibits: 5D 00477, and 5D 00478. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott, in reply quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, all I did so far was list the documents that I offered, so I think I'm entitled to a fair response. First of all, Your Honour, on the issue of that transcripts that were used or not used, Your Honour specifically encouraged us to offer all the transcripts through this witness and via this witness that he had -- did or could authenticate, and I took the Chamber's direction to heart and that's what I tried to do. If they are listed and tendered, the Defence can certainly raise any questions about them as they wished. If that's not the case and if the Prosecution relied on the direction of the Chamber to its prejudice and to its detriment, then in the future, Your Honour, I will just simply take more time with the witness, I'll make less of an effort to make the witness shorter rather than longer, and will make sure that we touch on every single document listed, if that's how we have to proceed. I did not understand from the Court's direction that that was the case with this witness, and we stand by tendering all the exhibits which I read to the Chamber earlier. The -- in terms of the book, Your Honour, the -- the book is the book. By that I mean I suppose there is no book that's been written in history that there wouldn't be someone somewhere which would say something was misstated in the book or something was left out of the book, but that is the book Mr. Manolic wrote. It is the book. It's not maybe the book that the Defence wishes he would have written, but it's his book that he wrote and that's the book that we have that's been tendered. I suppose it's a little bit like someone sitting here listening to these arguments, it's bit like someone who offered to put the Bible into evidence and then someone objecting, well, you can't do that because the Judas gospel isn't included, so therefore it shouldn't be admitted because there was something left out. Well, that's a dispute for the ages, Your Honour, but the point is the book is the book. Now, counsel has made certain objections to -- to the content of the book, which are fair comment, which they can argue, which they've argued today, they can argue in the future, but that does not go, in our submission, to the admissibility of the book itself. The book has been offered in its entirety. In terms of translations, Your Honour, the Court knows that this institution is grossly overburdened on translations. There are not enough translation resources to go around. There are many cases and many trials where translations -- there is a backlog of translations. There are many parts of longer documents, frankly, which some of them are clearly not relevant. An example came up with the presidential transcript the other day. There were pages and pages that went on about other domestic issues, introduction of the kuna, other things about trade agreements. There is no reason, in our respectful submission, Your Honour, to take scarce translation resources and devote those resources to translating irrelevant material, which means that -- sorry. Judge Prandler is encouraging me to slow down. Thank you, Judge. I just remind the Chamber that everything that's translated for this courtroom or for this trial means that something else in some other trial in some other case is not getting translated, and I think it's -- it's not a reasonable use of scarce resources to translate irrelevant material. Now, having said that, the point is this: The Defence has this material. They have had the material for some time. The Manolic book is well known. They certainly knew that that book would feature, and I invite them to submit any additional translations of the relevant parts which -- for translation that they would like to do. So, Your Honour, that's our position. I think all the exhibits that we've tendered should be admitted for the reasons stated. As to the Defence exhibits that have been tendered -- I should say before I do that, Your Honour, there were two -- before I close on the Prosecution exhibits, I know there are at least two that were specifically used by the Defence, including P 00699, and P 01452. So those were used by the Defence if not by the Prosecution itself and may have been used by both, I'm not sure at the moment, but they were certainly used by the Defence. The -- depending on the Court's ruling as applies to the Prosecution, I would note that the Defence marked and have tendered the following exhibits, which apparently were not used or presented to the witness, and that is: 3D 00319, 3D 00320, 3D 00305, 3D 00307, 3D 00145, 3D 00011, and 3D 00142. And I note for the record that at the least two documents were put to the witness, I believe by the Praljak Defence, which were given no number, and I don't know what the status of those documents are. I'm not familiar with the practice of showing documents to a witness for which no exhibit number is given, but I know that happened on at least two occasions with the witness. As to Exhibit 3D 00295, the Prosecution objects to its admission. This is the alleged handwritten note on Europcar stationery. There's been no adequate foundation or authentication of this document. We don't know where it came from. And the Chamber may remember that document as, Mr. President, you yourself raised some questions about it, and until there's further foundation for that document, we object to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President. With respect to the book, the Prosecution offered it in its entirety. Now, if this was an English book, a book in English, or say German, or say Hungarian, or say in French, I suspect those who could read those languages would read the entire book or would have access to the entire book as opposed to a portion of it. We heard a great deal of Mr. Manolic's testimony. His book tracks his political career. All of it is suspect, as far as we are concerned, particularly in light of his past in the sort of services, as they call it. Secondly, I believe Ms. Alaburic was -- was quite right in pointing out that the -- the interviews in there have been redacted. Also, if you might recall, Mr. President, there was one example by the Coric Defence counsel where it was shown to the -- to the witness where he'd given an interview and then he wanted the interviewee [sic] to redact a certain portion of it. Obviously given the nature of his personality, being a spy or in the services from the Tito era, the gentleman believes that's the way to conduct business. Also, you may recall, when I began my cross-examination I tried to pinpoint to the gentleman the fact that he owns the copyrights. This is Manolic on Manolic, so therefore I believe he's distorted his previous interviews and therefore it has very little probative value. Now, I understand that everything can be introduced, but at least if it is going to be introduced, I -- I hope that the Trial Chamber takes into consideration the fact that he has self-edited his prior statements in the press, and this is his book, it's not a book by a journalist on Mr. Manolic, and so I take -- so I would ask that. One thing I think I need to -- to -- to discuss, Mr. Scott indicated that the Praljak Defence team said they marked and they tendered certain documents but which were not used. They marked the documents, as I understand it. They weren't tendered because they weren't shown to the witness. And I don't know what the purpose behind that comment was, but I suggest -- I take it what the Prosecution is saying is any time a document is marked by the Defence and is presented to the other side without necessarily being shown to the witness, that document should come in. I don't believe that's the rule. If it is the rule, we certainly need some guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just two remarks. Colleague Scott has said -- said that the proposed book was written by Josip Manolic. Had this book been translated in its entirety, the Prosecutor would know that that book was not written by Josip Manolic. As a matter of fact, not a single word in the book was written by Josip Manolic. That book consists of parts of published interviews and of an historic text which is a sort of a commentary, and that historic text was not written by Josip Manolic but by Dragutin Hlad, who is indicated here as the person who prepared the book, a person that Manolic also confirmed himself that he had not written those comments. By the nature of things, Manolic could not have written his own interviews. So this is not a book written by Josip Manolic. And secondly, here we are not -- the Defence is not objecting to the admission of this book, if we take the Biblical example, because the Bible does not contain Judas gospel but, by paraphrasing this comment, we can say that the Prosecutor is invoking a Bible which does not contain a gospel by Luke, and he is claiming that this is an entire Bible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe I have to provide you an additional explanation in view of my colleague's comments. First of all, the Prosecution is against the introduction of 3D 002 -- 00320, which is a book by Miroslav Tudjman, "The Truth About Bosnia-Herzegovina," which chapters 1 to 5 published for the public and publicised all the relevant documents, different agreements, bilateral, multi-lateral, what have you, from the war period, which can provide one with proper insight into the developments at the time. So first of all, one agreement was proposed, the second agreement, the third agreement. All these agreements are relevant to this case. And, Your Honour, we will -- we will be obtaining all these agreements in this way or another -- one way or another, but the thesis which was advanced here, and which is why these agreements should have been presented to the witness, is that the witness was a big expert on Croatian policy towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, but when you ask him anything which went outside the scope of the business of the presidential office in Zagreb, or when you presented to him any document which did not refer to that same topic, in brief, his -- in a nutshell, his response was, "I don't know." So that very fact that he would have responded to all 220 documents, "I don't know," or "I don't know the details," shows that this is not a relevant piece of evidence, that the witness either doesn't know or pretends not to know what he's talking about, because if he does know the Croatian policy vis-a-vis Bosnia and Herzegovina, he ought to be aware of some at least the principle bilateral or multi-lateral agreements that were concluded. At that point, of course, with every justification, the Court intervened, and it was obvious at that point that we could not show the witness all these documents one by one and so that it was implied that the entire book could be tendered. Talking about the burden of the translation service, we can tell you that we have already requested a translation of it, and we were refused because it was a book. Well, I claim that it is not a book because simply it is a compilation of different agreements. So that we adhere to this request that chapters 1 from 5 should be tendered into evidence and admitted and we shall seek to have them translated. As regards the other object -- numbers which the colleague objected to, these were six identical documents, identical in content. The differences were only in terms of time and locations, and the markings. These were documents about convoys of armaments going from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If you remember, I held all six of them in my hand. I said let us put one of them on the ELMO. All the parties and the Court received -- were presented those documents, or if there had been any questions, they could have been raised at the time. So that I think that in keeping with our past practice, these documents should indeed be tendered and admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As regards this objection the documents that have not been shown cannot be tendered, I have understood your instructions that, as you told Mr. Scott, that these documents need to be formally shown for the witness to confirm their authenticity, but the Prosecution failed to do that. As Mr. Scott has said that 00699 and 00452 are problematic, that means that still seven documents remain that have not been presented to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Trial Chamber shall rule on the admission, on the question of the admission of exhibits, and this will, of course, cover the exhibits that we discussed today, and that will be attended also by a decision on the previous witness, Hujdur. Before we bring the witness in, I should like to speak -- to address the accused to tell them that yesterday Mr. Praljak again took the floor after the statement of the witness. I should like to remind them that when the examination-in-chief is being conducted, cross-examination is conducted by the Defence counsel and only exceptionally the accused may be allowed to speak, not to speak about his own case but in order to provide us with some precise fact or piece of information in reference to what the witness has said. We have repeatedly said that the -- on a number of occasions a number of the accused have taken the floor to state and profess their innocence. There is no need for you to do this. You have done so in your written submissions, and there is no need for you to repeat this every time a witness speaks. Also, when you intervene in connection with a witness who is speaking about some specific facts, we want such interventions to actually refer to who, when, how. That is what counts, that is what matters, and not to ask questions regarding some personal sentiments, political attitudes, because where facts are concerned, we want to have precise data about precisely facts, and only after the -- all the evidence has been presented we shall be making the conclusions. So I'm sure that you're perfectly aware of what the sense of my words is. We have lost enough time, and there is no need to lose any more time. We have devoted over 45 minutes to exhibits. Now we shall bring in the witness who has been waiting outside for about half an hour now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. The Prosecution will soon finish with the examination-in-chief. There are several questions left. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cupina.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I forget to do this, I believe that the map that was marked by the witness - and I'll certainly be guided by the registry - but I believe the next In Court exhibit number would be 00026 as In Court exhibit number which we will tender as marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before we leave the question of the mosques, which is one of the places we left off yesterday when you were marking certain locations on the map, you have mentioned personally seeing several of the mosques that you have identified to the Judges as seeing those mosques being shelled by the HVO. Can you tell the Judges, at the time that you observed this, did you see any ABiH or Muslim military positions in or in the immediate vicinity of any of these mosques?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near the mosque at the top of Cernica and the Karadzoz-bey mosque, there were no positions of nor any military forces nor even of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness please be shown Exhibit P 09044 and specifically the photo which is marked ERN 02083624.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what that is and how it relates to your testimony yesterday about sniping.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the building of the Privredna Banka, the commercial bank of Sarajevo, or the glass building, as people in Mostar used to call it, and from these positions they shelled civilians and other persons in the zone of responsibility of the HB H -- ABH army [as interpreted]. Actually, they sniped at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I next ask you to look, please --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me just add this: Already on the 18th of April, 1993, my brother Mirad Cupina was on duty in the command of the brigade, and they reported from Sanic's company that a man had been killed by a sniper, a citizen of Mostar at that locality, and also that in the streets right next to the court Slavko Cavar I believe was also killed by a sniper. That is also the testimony of my brother, and I myself would like to confirm that that happened at that time during what the Muslim people used to call the sniper war prosecuted by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to next look, and for the witness to be shown also part of the same exhibit, P 09044, but specifically photo ERN 02083625, which I see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This position is the Hotel Bristol, or a bridge whose name was changed from Musala to Tito's Bridge just prior to the war and during the war itself. This bridge was erected by international forces. This is the Hotel Bristol. The street's name is the street of the Mostar Battalion. It was constantly under sniper fire from the direction of the Aleksa Santic high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were there occasions, sir, where -- during the war where you crossed this bridge?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I often crossed this bridge because eminent people from Mostar needed to inspect and tour the lines, and I was a renown citizen of Mostar having been awarded awards, sports awards, so it was logical that I should too go and see the lines. Just behind the hotel, the Bristol Hotel, there was a company, and when I crossed over by car I know that I barely escaped alive. I often also went there behind Cernica to Mirza Hadziomerovic's flat. My building was on the Bulevar, so I had a flat there which I had been allotted as a deserved -- deserving citizen of Mostar, and it burnt. My flat burnt on the 9th of May, 1993, and it was precisely across this bridge that I managed to pull out my family, my wife and my children, and some of my neighbours to safety, which is to say to the left bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was normally -- that took place under sniper fire. There was a wholesale attack by the HVO at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have -- I think, just so the record is clear, I need to show the witness the map again on the ELMO. If I can have the usher's assistance. IC 00026. Sir, just a moment ago, and it's no longer on the screen, you referred again to the top -- excuse me, to the mosque at the top of Cernica street. On your map, using the numbers, which mosque were you referring to at the time when you say at the top of Cernica?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the top of Cernica it is mosque number A. It is on Adema Buca Street. It is this mark 1, marked by 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I think we've finished with that. Thank you, Madam Usher. Sir, if we could possibly just try to clarify a couple of things from yesterday. From 19 September, 1991, you were a reserve member of the civilian police in Mostar, having been activated during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. My wartime schedule, assignment was the war station of the police of the Ministry of the Interior of B and H.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us again very briefly, sir, because we're trying to finish your direct examination this morning, please, where was this war station approximately located in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was opposite the bus station, the city -- the municipal bus station, or the railway station, and it is the local commune called Carina. It is near the Carinski Most, or the Customs Bridge, in translation. It is just to the north. Some 200 metres from that place is the North Camp, the northern camp, which is the largest camp -- which was the largest Yugoslav People's Army camp or, rather, barracks of the army in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cupina. If we could move forward, I just want to touch on -- you mentioned several times in your testimony yesterday something called the Patriotic League. And before we conclude, I'd like you to tell the Judges a bit more. What was the Patriotic League and when was it formed in the Mostar region?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Patriotic League. That is an organisation which was charged with bringing Bosnia and Herzegovina into -- steering it into calm waters so as -- for it to be recognised by the international community. In the Patriotic League were all the peoples and citizens who were anti-fascists. People and citizens of Mostar, of course. From the lists of the captured people which remained in the HVO, you can see the names of such people and anti-fascist citizens. Our task was to do this for Mostar and Bosnia and Herzegovina, but HVO wouldn't let us because units came -- kept coming from Croatia and engaged in various diversions, and I can tell you that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please stop there for a moment, sir. When you said -- you said that you can see names of such people, our task was to do this. When you say "this," what does that mean? The task was to do what? Tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our task, the task of the Patriotic League was to, by peaceful means, calm down the situation in Mostar and bring us into a situation whereby we would be internationally recognised as Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, was the Patriotic League also engaged in preparing to defend itself and arming itself against the Serb aggression?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Patriotic League waged a liberation and defensive war to save home -- one's home, one's neighbours' homes, and so on. And it also took part in arming the people. All the people and citizens who did not wish to allow Greater Serbia to be created on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to move on now. Can you tell the Chamber, was there a time when something in Mostar called the Independent Battalion was formed, and what was that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the first aggressive operations in the southern reaches of the city, I think that already on the 1st of April the JNA and the reservists launched an aggressive onslaught against Mostar, 1992, so that we emerged on the 4th of April from our underground operations because after the explosion of the water truck in front of North Camp and the north barracks of the JNA in the Zalik district.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the relationship, if any, between the -- what had been the Patriotic League and the Independent Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Independent Battalion was the reserve force of the police and all the patriotic forces who were bent on preventing the creation of Greater Serbia and protection of the AVNOJ borders, Anti-fascist Council of National Liberation borders, of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did the Independent Battalion participate in the liberation of Mostar from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Independent Battalion did participate in the liberation of Mostar. However, we did not come upon support from the HVO, because in the northern part, several kilometres away, about five kilometres away, there was an enclave populated mostly by Muslims. We had -- we did not have support of the HVO, and what support we did was very weak. And they had already had an agreement, reached an agreement with the Serbs or, rather, Boban and Karadzic kept agreeing to the detriment of the Muslims in Mostar, and we did not receive adequate aid and assistance. What we had were ordinary rifles. I think I had two machine-guns, one at the entrance to Mostar and the other in the south, and one RPG at Vrh, and all that to fight a corps that was called the Bileca Corps. So we were insufficiently trained and insufficiently armed. We had no logistical back-up either because they blackmailed us and said unless we joined the HVO, we would get nothing. They would withdraw and let the Chetniks slaughter us and that then they would reach an agreement with the Chetniks as to how to divide Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I would like to interrupt you because you are -- first of all, I believe you speak very fast. Secondly, I wonder if you are reading a text, because if you do, I believe you have to speak up from your own thoughts. So okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He's not reading, Your Honour. These are memorised lines that he's been given to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, what's the basis for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's nothing in the statement about any of this. Nothing. There's nothing in the statement between 1992 and 1993, none of this. This is all brand new stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We've covered this yesterday, Your Honour. I'm not going to go back through it again unless the Court directs me to. We've been through what was in the statement and not in the statement. The witness has nothing in front of him; I can see from here. He's giving his evidence. And I object. Once again, Mr. Karnavas always jumps to the most negative possible interpretation of any event in the courtroom, and I object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, just -- go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the answer, I don't think there's any doubt that that is not contained in the statement. The subject is not in the statement. It's something new that we're hearing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask two -- one clarifying question and one additional question to close, I hope, on the issue of the Independent Battalion. So the record is clear, a few moments ago - and again it's no longer on the screen - you mentioned that the Muslim forces this time were in opposition, standing in opposition to I think something called the Bileca -- I may have mispronounced that - B-i-l-e-c-a - Corps, and just so the record is clear, of what armed formation or military force was the Bileca Corps?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bileca Corps was led by Momcilo Perisic, general of the Yugoslav People's Army, and Pusara. That was the 10th Motorised Brigade. It was the position of North Camp, or north barracks, and there was a military base, an air force base, planes and helicopters in Jasenica, Ortesje [phoen], Rodoca, in that area, and then there were paramilitary formations, then there was the Nevesinje Brigade, the Bileca, Trebinje Brigades --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and all the brigades --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We need to move forward, please. My last question about the Independent Battalion was did the Patriotic League in the Mostar region continue to exist after the Independent Battalion was formed or not? Or was it folded into the Independent Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the point when Bosnia-Herzegovina received recognition, when we created an army, when we had our own MUP, there was no need for the Patriotic League any more and the legal organs of the state took over the defence and liberation war in the Mostar area or, rather, throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. First of all, there was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, which leads me to my next question: Can you tell the Judges, if you know, when the 4th Corps of the ABiH was formed.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Corps of the ABiH was formed, I think, on the 16th or 17th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, again, what had been the Independent Battalion or was the Independent Battalion, was that then moved into or became part of the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Independent Battalion was active until the 13th of July, 1992, or thereabouts, and it grew to become the 1st Mostar Brigade. And the 1st Mostar Brigade was composed of corps and companies and other units from the territory of Mostar municipality and further afield.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, with the usher's assistance, can the witness please be shown Exhibit P 00229. Sir, if you see that document, can you tell the Judges what that document is; and again is this one of the documents that you collected and transmitted to the Sarajevo government during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the document, or one of the documents, and I can explain why we had this: Because we lost positions on the left bank, and since in the southern reaches of Mostar all the houses were set on fire, the fighters and their families were left without homes and houses, and in that part of Mostar there were about 1.000 military flats belonging to the military, and our men, our people who were left homeless, moved into those flats. Now, to prevent that, they issued this order, and all the inhabitants of Mostar rose in opposition to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the usher please scroll down just so the witness and others can see the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to next look, sir, and the witness to be shown Exhibit P 00488.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time -- at that same time, we had some informal information which stated that they were doing that because they wanted to displace people in a humane way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I don't think there is a question pending at the moment. If Mr. Scott wishes this information, perhaps he would ask a question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you have any other information about these events at that time you can share with the Chamber about the order, the document we were just looking at? 00488. The one that was just on the -- excuse me. I'm sorry. 00229 is the one we were just looking at. Sir, did you receive any other information around this time about the implementation of this decision which is marked P 00229?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, as I said a moment ago, things happened that way. We had problems about putting these people up. They wanted to prevent it, and the conclusion was -- this conclusion was issued, stating who could move into the flats and who couldn't. And first of all, it was people who had signed a document and took the oath could move in. People who were members of the HVO were given priority. And then anything left over was given to the others. They did not allow the army to dispose of the flats, although they were municipal flats belonging to the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those flats belonged to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for interrupting, but I think that the question gave rise to speculation, and the witness has -- was asked for the reasons for which this decision was taken, how they -- what guided them to bring in this decision. The witness can't know that. He can only speculate. So the question opened the door for speculation. We are interested in who, what, when and how. So could this be clarified, who, what, when and how, because otherwise we're going to lose half an hour in the cross-examination on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, a moment ago you said that people had to sign some sort of a document and take some sort of an oath. What document had to be signed and what oath had to be taken?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oath of allegiance, stating their allegiance to the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know the -- remember the actual wording of the text, but that was the oath of allegiance that they were asked to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I just heard you say in both Herceg-Bosna and then Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you say which -- to what entity were they asked to take an oath of allegiance?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The oath of allegiance to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council of Mostar municipality. And that was a parastate, a state within the state. A state within the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which meant the disintegration of all the institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You also mentioned a moment ago that you said something to the effect - and again we don't have it on the screen now - but they wouldn't allow the army to distribute or allocate the housing units. When you said that, which army were you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to -- well, the flats belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, but the BH army and the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have the right to dispose of those flats, because the sole right to dispose of them was taken over by the leaders of Herceg-Bosna or the Croatian defence community in Mostar municipality for all the empty flats, all the flats that had been left empty in Mostar and the surrounding regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, now I would like to move forward to Exhibit P 00488.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apparently, Your Honour, I'm told that -- I've just been told that the English version in e-court apparently there is some problem with it. I'm not sure exactly what the problem is, but if we can put the hard copy on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can see that document. Once again, can you tell us what that is, please; and if you recognise it, can you tell the Judges once again whether this is one of the documents that you collected and transmitted to the BH government?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is the rules of procedure on the protection of refugees and displaced persons on the territory of Mostar municipality. That was the Croatian Defence Council's rules, that this should be applied to displaced persons and refugees. About 17.000 people who had come in from the territory of Eastern Herzegovina, and that is territory which the SAO of Eastern Herzegovina, as it was called, it expelled these people, and sometime on the 16th of June they found themselves in Mostar. However, the leadership of the HVO was opposed to this and they brought in a large column of buses to expel those people, to take them to Zenica, because they said that wasn't the agreement we reached, you must go to your own canton or district, which the intellectuals of Mostar found unacceptable and opposed it, and the Ministry of the Interior supported us, as did the BH army. And that convoy was stopped and our people -- or, rather, the refugees and dispelled persons did not end up in Zenica but they stayed in Mostar. So those buses were located in front of the pupils' centre, the Djacki Dom. It's like a boarding school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness to next be shown, please, Exhibit P 00485. Sir, I'll again ask you if you recognise the document, and again if this is a document that you collected and transmitted --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Judges what this document is.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina no longer existed and that all power and authority -- and that the state of Bosnia didn't exist and all the power and authority was vested in the parastate of the HZ HB and the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, which meant that they deleted all the documents of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina by this decision and placed everything under the control of their own units and departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, clearly the witness is, to say the least here, venturing a legal analysis of the contents of this document and its effect. Your Honour, that's completely inadmissible and I object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown Exhibit P 00490. P 00490.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Once again, sir, do you recognise that document and can you tell the Judges whether that is a document that you collected and provided to the BH government?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And ever so briefly, sir, what is that document about, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- it's, as we can see -- I don't know if it's the integral document. It relates to the Croatian Defence Council of the 5th of June. They took over all the enterprises in Mostar and placed all their own people, as far as I can see, all their directors, or whatever they call them; managers, directors, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can find on the page, sir, in the -- excuse me, Your Honour. Can you look at the item on the page which is number 01-1745/92. My apologies. I didn't realise there were multiple documents on the B/C/S page. Would you look at that particular document and tell us what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you zoom down, please? I can't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Upper-left corner on the screen, I believe, Mr. Cupina. Number 0 -- Broj 01-1745/92. And the text is above that.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the document lower down, please? I can't see that portion on the document. As far as I know, this deals with flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just a moment. Can we move the picture -- the screen -- the image down, the -- no, the other direction. The opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the top. The top. So I can see the top. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Up a bit. Keep going. Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir -- just please, ever so briefly, tell us only -- so what was this document about, now that we have the right one in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The flats which were vacated by the previous occupants are given over to the HVO who, on the basis of set criteria, will give them over to the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, or flats belonging to the national defence previously. Now, what did that mean? Due to the war operations, many people -- many citizens of Mostar left the city of Mostar. They left with bags, all their belongings in their bags, and left behind their flats. Some people did so of their own free will, others were forced to leave because the military police stormed their flats and took the people away to what was the -- called the Celovina prison, an investigative prison, and to the university of Dzemal Bijedic. And people also left Mostar, saving their lives. Now, the other flats, the remaining flats, were used by them. That was their exclusive right. So many flats were left empty, and the other people who left their flats were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Obviously the witness isn't answering the question. The question took quite another direction. Now we have the witness giving lengthy explanations about something that has nothing to do with what he was asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said a moment ago, sir, that there -- there was a reference to the military police expelling people. The military police, sir, of what armed force? Whose military police was involved in this?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police of the HVO, and I think the commander at the time was Zeljko Dzidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you said -- and you also said "them." Hold on one moment, please. Hold on. "Now, the other flats, the remaining flats were used by them. That was their exclusive right." So who is the "them" you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean about those flats. The JNA. Those flats, the JNA flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The JNA flats. A moment ago, sir, you said -- I'm looking at page 34, line 22, "Now, the other flats, the remaining flats were used by them." Who is the "them" you're referring to? Who you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first lot of flats, well, the HVO used them to bring in their own people in this humane way of resettling them, because Ante Valenta, the creator of the book on humane resettlement laid the grounds for that. We knew that that was something that was being prepared because mention of that was made already in 1991 and 1992 to the effect that certain people from Kakanj, Vares, and so on, would be resettled around Stolac, and this was really put into practice. And I remember at those meetings they spoke about a settlement in the area of Mostar Blato [phoen] being set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... non-responsive to the question, and we have no way of telling what area he's going to go into and to make appropriate objections. Will Mr. Scott please ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in terms of the collection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, would you please limit your examination to questions of substance, because we've gone into talking about Kakanj, Vares, Stolac, and so on. We're branching out the now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned yesterday and again today the collection and transmission of various documents and reports to the BH government, and an issue was raised yesterday in reference to the time of the decisions issued by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you tell the Judges, please, were you collecting and transmitting documents throughout 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time and I've got a few more minutes, if the Court would take a break here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the registrar to give me the time that the Prosecutor has taken thus far. Well, we can continue for another few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you -- did you ever have any conversations with various of the accused in this case concerning the status of the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with most of the accused here I had conversations, yes. In May, 1992, I already spoke -- or Coric sent me a private letter, he calls it a private letter, to the effect that we were poorly armed, poorly organised, and that the HVO knows about that, they know how you should wage a struggle, and that -- and I understood it that we should leave all power and authority to the HVO for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I couldn't allow that to happen. And they all said that it was the state of Herceg-Bosna and that it would be conjoined to a Greater Croatia or, rather, Croatia, that the Drina River would not be the border but that the border would be on the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, sir. Let me ask you specifically: Did you have a conversation about -- any conversation about these matters with Mr. Jadranko Prlic and, if so, tell us briefly about that conversation, and specifically address -- please specifically address your comment to that question.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the Dzemal Bijedic University in November was practically dismantled, the university was established, I think that the dean was Kordic, November, 1992, is the date we're talking about, and I went to Siroki Brijeg, the former Listica, to the premises of the Franciscan monastery on a hill, and there were exams being held there. I went to see Mr. Prlic, and in a conversation, he told me that this area would be called Herceg-Bosna. There would be a parastate within a state, and that the HVO were the only representatives in the area, et cetera. He said things to the effect that we as Muslims had no claims that we could make. He said we should go to our enclaves. I think he mentioned Zenica, Sarajevo, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations during this time period with either Mr. Coric and Mr. Stojic in -- well, let me say, did your brother -- excuse me. Was your brother taken into custody by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, around the 18th of April, 1993, having been on guard in the corps or the brigade, my brother returned home and I think that the president of the football club, Bijeljic Milo [phoen], took him in, brought him in. He took him to the prison in the faculty of mechanical engineering. His wife knew nothing about him for about two days. Then I went to see Bruno Stojic, and Coric -- Valentin Coric as a result. I asked my brother was. I assumed that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... where did you go to see Mr. Coric and Stojic; at what location?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the headquarters at the end of the avenija, or avenue, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, if you recall, where were the offices of Mr. Coric and Mr. Stojic at that time in relation to one another?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was the secretary's office between their offices. Bruno Stojic was to the left, and Coric was to the right. I arrived there and said that I had come to ask about the whereabouts of my brother and about who had arrested him. I asked him to release him by 12.00. I think it was quite hot at the time, and I had this conversation. My brother was released at 12.00, and naturally he had his own story to tell. He said that he had been in prison with his neighbour Jovo Srvla [phoen] and with a member of what they call the MOS, the Muslim armed forces. They said that they had tied his hands and arms up, that they had -- that there were other people there. He can give you a statement as to who was there in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an Albanian too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, thank you. We have time limitations. Sir, for the final couple of questions, can you tell us -- you talked about various meetings and conversations with Mr. Pusic yesterday. Did you ever meet or talk with Mr. Pusic in connection with the Muslim men who had been taken from the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us about that conversation, please.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had such conversations when exchanges were being discussed. We talked about all these matters. He was very decisive. He pretended not to know anything, and he practically refused to discuss this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... attention specifically to the Vranica building now. Did you speak or meet with Mr. Pusic about the Muslim men that had been taken from the Vranica building on the 10th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us what was said in that regard.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he knew nothing about them. He didn't know where they were, how they had been taken away, although I personally know that he was the be-all and end-all, the alpha and the omega, and he knew about the whereabouts of each detainee in Mostar and he knew when they should be released and in what manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say the alpha and omega, the alpha and omega, to use your terms, in reference to what?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reference to prisoners, the citizens of Mostar, the people, because all citizens of Mostar who were against the HZ HB and the HVO were arrested and placed in these concentration camps naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Finishing on this, did there come a time in approximately September, 1993, that you left Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the governmental delegation arrived in Mostar, I think it was headed by Enver Kreso, Omer Basic, and Hajrudin Sumar [phoen], they suggested that I go to Sarajevo with them with their sons -- with my sons, who were 8 and 12 years old, and with my wife I went to Sarajevo via the mountains and was accommodated with the president of the region, Mr. Mustafa Pamuk. This is a flat located right next to President Izetbegovic's flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you just briefly tell us, because the Judges have heard, I think, some references to this, how did you travel from Mostar to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through Bijelo Polje. We used a mountain path to get from Mostar to Jablanica. You spend a night in the mountains and then continue on foot. You could only carry a few things with you because -- well, we practically had no water, no food, but we reached Jablanica, and then I moved on to Sarajevo through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cupina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution has now concluded its examination-in-chief of the witness. The Prosecution took up two hours and 40 minutes, so we have another four hours and 30 minutes because we've got an hour and 30 and then a few more hours this afternoon. If the Defence counsel hasn't reached an agreement, each team has 45 minutes, but if you have reached an agreement on the order that you will be following, use up your time as you see fit. But the Defence counsel has four hours and 30 minutes in total. If you haven't reached an agreement, each Defence team has 45 minutes. We will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the floor to Defence counsel now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. On behalf of the Defence, I'd like to inform Your Honours that we have agreed on the time and on the order we'll follow. I will start first, and I'll work until the break. We'll use the time you have given us, and after the break I will inform you of the order we will follow, if that is of importance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cupina, my name is Senka Nozica. I am a lawyer from Sarajevo. I'll have some questions for you on behalf of Mr. Bruno Stojic. The Prosecution asked you about the Patriotic League today in Mostar. You provided a detailed answer, but you didn't say when the Patriotic League was formed in Mostar, nor did you say what your role in the Patriotic League was.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Patriotic League in Mostar was formed around -- or when the Serbs arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Cupina, I'll put very simple and brief questions to you. I want to know the date, the month, the year.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not the accused here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You are the witness here.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my own way of speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You have to answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not an accused here, but you have to answer the questions put to you. The accused mustn't be subject to prejudice because of the witnesses, so please answer the questions put to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When was the Patriotic League in Mostar formed?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Serbian and Montenegro reservists arrived in Mostar, on the 19th of September. That's around -- that's about the date when the war started. The 19th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 1991. What was the Patriotic League in fact?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an organisation that protected the interests of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's what you said. My question is very concrete: Was it established on the initiative of the SDA part? Was it the military wing of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So your answer is affirmative. If it was the military wing of the SDA party, who were its members in Mostar? Were they members of other ethnic groups, non-Muslim ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: They were?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How long did those other members remain members of the Patriotic League, and can you provide me with at least one name of such people, for example, in Mostar, the members of the Crisis Staff of the Patriotic League? You write about this in your book. Can you provide me with a single name that is not the name of a Bosniak or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Crisis Staff? Well, the Crisis Staff was formed by the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm not talking about. I'm talking about the Crisis Staff of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the whole the members were Muslims; but there was Fink, Duzdevic, Dejanic [phoen], et cetera, who were members and who had important roles to play in the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Many such people were in the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, you said today that the Mostar Independent Battalion was established on the 4th of April, 1991. That's when it ceased to be an illegal entity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you a member of this Independent Mostar Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was its commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As of when?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the time it was established up until the 15th of May, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So that means from the 14th of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Afterwards you became the commander of the military police from the 12th of June, 1992, and you were never relieved of those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for the interruption. Perhaps it's correct, but twice now in the transcript the witness has said -- and both the question and the answer has been indicated 1991, and I'm wondering whether it wasn't -- 1992 wasn't the intended date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ask the witness for the precise date, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. As far as the Patriotic League is concerned, the witness said 1991. When we discussed the Mostar Independent Battalion --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said the Patriotic League was formed in 1991, and the Independent Battalion was on the 4th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. You were the commander of the military police as of the 12th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was never relieved of those duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. The president of the commission of -- for exchanges, you had that role from the 21st -- 25th of May until June, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a report was made. It was up until July, 7th of July, I think. On the 8th of July, I became a commissioner for the company Energopetrol, but a report was compiled then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On the 8th of July you became a commissioner for Energopetrol.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When did you leave Mostar for good?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in September. I have it in my files. I have a document in my files that shows the date I left Mostar and went to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Which month are we talking about and which year?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1993, and I think it was in September or August. I can't remember exactly. There's a document which I can provide you with.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you arrived in Sarajevo, were you involved in the military?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I then became a selector of the Bosnia and Herzegovina team.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you anything about that. We'll discuss sport later on. You said that you were appointed or, rather, promoted to the rank of officer in 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is correct. The Presidency adopted that decision. Nad kapetan, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And from 1993 to 1996 -- can we say that from July 1993 until 1996 you weren't involved in the military, you weren't engaged in the military?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we conclude that from July 1993 until 1996 you were not engaged in the military?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you can draw that conclusion, but I received that rank from the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about your rank, but can we draw the conclusion that you weren't engaged in the military as of July, 1993, up until 1996? The answer is simple; yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in my military booklet I wrote down that I'd been engaged in the military for 18 months.
