utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if I've understood you correctly, the office that you worked in was not far from this facility, this -- this bank. Could you confirm that your office was next to the bank or not far from it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On the 21st of May, were you in your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were not aware of the fact that several metres away there were at least 39 individuals who were being held as prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really had no information about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, it's as if we had a prison just across the road from this building, and now you're telling us that you had no knowledge about this. That's what you're telling us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was the command of the 4th Corps that was there and of the Mostar Brigade. That's all I knew about it. If that's what you're referring to, if that's what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But according to what you say, if it's true, your task was to exchange prisoners, to organise prison exchanges, exchanges of HVO and ABiH prisoners. That was your mission, your task, and now we learn that there were some prisoners being held in detention several metres away from where you had your office and now you're saying you know nothing about this, you knew nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's absolutely certain. I never knew anything about this until there was this exchange of these two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the name Igor Kapor, which appears in your report, where did this name come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, his name was mentioned at the exchange itself. As far as I know, I can remember him and Suad Nametak. I didn't have any other information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're the president of the Commission for Exchanges, and you were told that someone called Igor Kapor is being held by one of the sides, and you didn't even ask yourself where he was being detained, where he was detained?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even know that he was being held as a prisoner until this issue was raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me the following: You said that you didn't know that Igor Kapor or these individuals were detained, at least not until this issue was raised. Were you provided with a list of individuals that the Croatian side was looking for? When you were in the commission, did you see any such lists?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I didn't see lists of any kind. I don't know if they provided lists to someone else, perhaps to Arif Pasalic, but I can't remember being provided with lists of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: But later on, did you see such lists? Did Arif Pasalic inform you of such lists since you were his deputy?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. They did their work and we were separate in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I don't understand what your work involved, in that case. I just don't understand that. What were your duties? I fail to understand.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, what were my duties?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: What were your duties? You have no knowledge about lists, you know nothing about detainees. They were walking around on the left bank of Mostar. You have to help me because I can't understand you.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you everything that I know about.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, could we come to the conclusion that in fact you know absolutely nothing about exchanges? You have no knowledge about lists, you have no knowledge about where these people were being held, you don't know whether they were imprisoned or whether they were free. You have absolutely no knowledge about the exchanges; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, tell me what you know.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you everything I know. You've seen that in the report I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Your report is contradictory. It contradicts what you said because you mention prisoners in your report and in your testimony you say there were no prisons. If a person is detained, a prisoner, then either he's being held in a prison or in a concentration camp. Such persons don't walk around Mostar. How can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the report was compiled. It is such as it is, and I know nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: But we can't understand this, given your testimony.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the report that I drafted, and things were as I have said, and I don't know how to put it in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I can't obtain an answer to this question. I'll move on since it's obvious that I won't obtain an answer. We don't have much time. Could we see document 5D 00494, please. In the heading of this document, it says the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council, operative zone of South-eastern Herzegovina, Mostar, the date is Mostar, the 23rd of May, 1993. The title of the document is the list of HVO members being held in prison by the ABiH, the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. Could we now have a look at the following page. I think it's page number 3. Yes. Could you scroll up a bit, please. A little further. A little further down, in fact. That's fine. That's good. On page 3 we can see that it says "civilians," and then we have a list of the civilians concerned. I won't read through it. And it says next to the name of each individual, each civilian, "In prison in Jablanica." Do you have any knowledge about that prison?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I never even went to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether there was a prison in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how would I know that? We couldn't communicate with Jablanica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt my colleague. I think the witness still has in front of him some other documents left over from the former cross-examination. Perhaps those could be taken away at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please remove your documents. Yes. That's good. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cupina, I'll now show a number of documents to you and then I'll ask you a general question about all those documents. Could we see document 5D 00479. The heading says the operative zone of South-eastern Herzegovina, OZ JIH, the SIS department, then we have a number, Mostar, the 30th of April, 1993. The title of the document is information, or report. I'll only read out part of the document. I'm reading the second paragraph out now: "In a series of attacks on individuals and groups of Croats and HVO members on which occasions they were maltreated, insulted, and physically abused, their property would be taken away from them, et cetera, but our attention is drawn in particular to the event that took place on the 27th of April, 1993. In fact, at a checkpoint next to the tobacco factory, certain town inhabitants, Zijo Orucevic, Emir Habibija, Nermin Cupina, and Azer Penava, together with those town criminals intercepted three members of the HVO military police: Pero Delic, Marko Martinac, and Roland Martinic. They took their weapons from them and then they forced them to graze on the grass and to crawl along the asphalt road. This abuse was performed between 1930 hours and 2030 hours. "Since this is not the only form that the abuse of Croats has taken, it is necessary to do everything to protect the citizens and officials on the left bank. One form of fighting against such perpetrators or fighting against perpetrators of such act would be to issue a wanted list or, rather, to place them beyond the law." Do you know the individuals who have been mentioned here, Zijo Orucevic and the others that I have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zijo Orucevic and these other individuals were such criminals. They were "zulumcari."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you say what "zulumcari" means?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it means people who are fighting for themselves. They were with Tuta, and then they fought for someone else. Zijo Orucevic wounded me. Nermin Cupina was a petty criminal before the war near Mostar. Similarly, Emir Habibija was a petty criminal. He disturbed public law and order. I don't know who they were with, who they belonged to at the time, but they were young men who tended to disturb law and order.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So we have identified these people. You know who they are. Can we have 5D 00468 -- 86, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a question on this document. This is one Nermin Cupina. Is that a relative of yours? I have on this document one person by the name of Nermin Cupina. I wonder whether it is a relative of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he is not. He's from the village of Vranjevici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So we have the same heading. Let me not go through it all. It is the 7th of May, 1993. It is an extraordinary report, signed by the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the military police, Zeljko Dzidic. And the report which you have before you, and you can of course go through it, but if not, I'm going to summarise what it is about. This is about different incidents in which people came under fire, or fire was opened in the eastern part of Mostar. Fire was opened at HVO members in the eastern part of Mostar. This took place on the 7th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: There is no question. I just want to summarise the contents so that we save time, because this is of relevance to the consolidated question, the general question which I'm going to ask you. Can we move on to document 5D 00514.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you're now asking some preliminary questions. You are making a sort of introduction to your question. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Yes. Some associated documents which are mutually interconnected. At the end, I shall be asking a very brief question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. Continue. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So we have a document. It says the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council, the 3rd Battalion of the military police, crime suppression department, Mostar, the 7th of May, 1993. It's a special report, or extraordinary report, signed by two officers, Sifra [phoen] and Zelenika, and this describes an event of fire having been opened, and severe injuries having been sustained on the 7th of May, 1993, by 14 HVO members, and one of them was gravely injured and one indeed succumbed to his injuries. So this took place on the road leading to go Rodoc, the junction towards the Lucki Most. You are familiar with all these sites, so I spared you the reading for the sake of time. Can I ask that 5D 00485 be shown to the witness, please. It is the same heading as the previous documents apart from the last one. 2nd HVO Brigade, 7th May, 1993. This is a report on an on-site investigation, and the signature says that Ivan Pazin and Ivica Rotin conducted the investigation, and this is an on-site investigation of the previous incident of the opening of fire on the road towards Rodoc which I described a while ago. And now I come to my question. Are you familiar with any of the incidents that I mentioned here; the 30th of April, the 7th of May, and the 5th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard about -- I heard about this incident which took place at Donja Mahala. I heard that there were some skirmishes there. Some fire was exchanged with Juka, because allegedly some people said he had joined the HVO, crossed over to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So you did hear about these events?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: At that time you were the commander of the military police of the -- of the army of B and H. You were not still relieved of duty. You were an operative, as you said. You were the person in charge of the police for the Mostar area. In fact, you said for the entire area of Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only told you in my statement that I had a paper to that effect and I had no real powers nor any authority. I could not institute any proceedings because all the judicial organs were under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me just verify this. You said that the military police of the army of B and H under your command did not even manage to get organised because you were prevented from doing so by the HVO. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: 5D 00513 is the document I should like the witness to be shown now, please. The heading says Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council, 1st Company, the Tihomir Misic barracks, 12th of March, 1993, Mostar. The title is "Report on the organisation of the military police of the Tihomir Misic left bank barracks." I shall now read for you some parts of it. Can we go to the third paragraph, please, so that I don't read the entire document. The third paragraph says the following: "All the duties and movements of the army of the B and H and the military police of army report to our station and they seek approval from us. All apprehensions, the closure of facilities and other duties we have been conducting without any major problems. Whenever an incident or something similar happens, the army of BH and the military police of the army regularly seek us, our participation in it and report to us on it. For work and security on the left bank to be as successful as possible, we need to increase the number of policemen (50 to 60) as well as the number of soldiers in the barracks on the left bank. In order for all this to function as best as possible, you -- we need to set up another one or two checkpoints in the city itself. "For work to be as successful as possible, we also need to recruit -- to engage the civilian MUP on the left bank. All the duties regarding the -- all duties regarding civilians are being carried out by the military police so that the large need for a civilian ministry of the interior is filled. "On the left bank there already functions the civilian police of the army, and they are located in two or three places on the left bank." This is signed by the commander of the station of the military police, of the TM barracks, the commander of the 1st Company, Tihomir Misic. It seems to me that there existed a military police and that it cooperated with the ABiH. That is in 1993, a month before the incidents in question. Am I right? That is what it appears to me from this document.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the military police of the Mostar Brigade, but not of the region. I was only referring to the military police of the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not what you said, sir.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I misspoke. Perhaps I didn't say it all.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: But you said that the military police had not been organised as yet and that you didn't have any powers.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to that of the region, of the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Then we don't understand each other. Sir, you never referred to the region. You kept saying that you were the commander of the military police of the H -- BH and that it was personally Mr. Sefer Halilovic who had appointed you to that post.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I can find this for you in the transcript. Don't make me do that.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I give you an answer, please? What I said was it does say the commander of the military police of the region of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not what you said.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in the document. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not have any further questions for this witness. Thank you, Mr. Cupina. I should like to give the floor to Mr. Coric, by your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Cupina. I should like to read a portion of a document which we did not plan to tender today, just to show that the military police in the region of Herzegovina from Konjic to the south did exist and was organised not only at brigade level and corps level but also at regional level, at the level of the entire region. In the heading -- we shall be tendering this document when the first opportunity poses itself, but let us now just discuss the period it deals with. The heading is Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, command of the 4th Corps, security organ. The date is the 2nd of February, 1993. The document's title is report on the organisation of the formation of the battalion of the military police. It is addressed to the deputy commander for security affairs. And I'm just going to read a very short portion of the text. And this is with -- in reference to the documents present by Defence counsel a while ago. On the 15th of December, 1992 -- this previous document was of the 12th of March, 1993 -- the commander of the 4th Corps issued an order on the setting up of a battalion of -- of the military police of the 4th Corps of the army of B and H, appointing the commander of the military police battalion, Mr. Nusret Sahic. While the deployment of the battalion was to be such that one company would be stationed at Jablanica, one company in Mostar, and the command of the battalion and another company in Konjic. This order came into force with immediate effect on the day of its issuance. Mr. Cupina, does this document, this short extract of this document, which otherwise has two pages, does it disprove you, namely your statement that in the period under consideration there did not exist a regional police on the -- one of the decisions in reference to which also your name features? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document of Arif Pasalic of the 21st of March, 1993, attests to the fact that I did not set up --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask you that. Please answer my question. I don't have much time.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And a step further, to go a step further, I should like to speak about a document which regrettably also today emanates from what has been discussed today, but it will be much briefer for the one we discussed previously. It is also Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then it goes on to say battalion of the military police, the 27th -- 27th of January, 1993, namely the police has already been organised, set up, and is functioning. This document is signed by the Commander Nusret Sahic, and just one sentence from that document by which I wish to corroborate that not only did there exist a military police of the army of BH in the region of Mostar but also that it cooperated with the HVO; i.e., the military police of the HVO. And I quote from this document: "On the 26th and 27th of January, 1993, three people were killed in Brdjani and one in Buturovic Polje." Where are Brdjani and Buturovic Polje, Mr. Cupina?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Buturovic Polje I know is in the vicinity of Konjic. I don't know about this other place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me read out for you another sentence: "Together the police of the MUP and the HVO -- with the police and the MUP of the HVO, we inspected the scene of the events and on which there exist records that were drawn up." So that this -- this is a document of the battalion -- military police battalion, and when the opportunity poses itself, we shall be tendering this document into the case file. That is as far as the question of the military police is concerned. Mr. Cupina, I would like us to solve some problems now, ones that were raised yesterday that you spoke about. You mentioned a letter of mine that I sent to you sometime in May, 1992. Have you kept that letter?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to have it on you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the office of the Tribunal. I think it's there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Did you present that letter to Alija Izetbegovic personally during the first visit to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cupina, who brought you that letter?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember who brought the letter. One of your people. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I should now like to refer to your book. I'm going to have to read out a portion of the book. It is on page 486 and 487. "I was the target," you say, "of various manipulations with the aim of placing me to work for the politics of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. After my departure from the Independent Battalion and the defence of Mostar, a Bosniak delegation went to see Valentin Coric straight away, and also Bruno Stojic ..." Now, I'm interrupting the sentence there. There's a comma, and I'm going to continue later on. Can you remember whether anybody from the delegation brought you that letter of mine that I sent, since you can't remember the name?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to continue reading the sentence: " ... they accused me of me having accused and blamed the HVO because of the fall of the left bank ..." And I interrupt the sentence there again to ask you who are "they" when you say "they accuse me"?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Himzo Nazrajic and Stela, as far as I remember. They gave me that information, and some others I don't remember. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I never mentioned two names in that context, but you'll see what this is about when I read on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: And I'm continuing that sentence: "... they even asked that I be liquidated." Who asked for your liquidation?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people who came. You conveyed that to me, Valentin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: When and where?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Valentin, when you entered into the alliance with BH, or in a conversation. When I was at a competition in Citluk.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Cupina, what units Stela and Nazrajic were in at the time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please remind me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the Bosniak delegation which came to see me, and which came to see Bruno Stojic, as you say. As far as I know, those two men were never in any Bosniak delegation. If you have information to the contrary, who could they have belonged to? Tell us here and now.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You told me that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. And I'm going to read on from the book. You stated the following: That I told the delegation, that I said to them that we weren't in charge of the Bosniaks. "'You must do that yourselves ...'" that is to say to kill Cupina, that's what it means, just to make things clear. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: "'... if you're courageous enough,' Coric said to them, and subsequently one of the visitors acknowledged that later on." So you once again refer to these visitors. Obviously those were not Stela and Nazrajic. So if it wasn't clear to you the first time or the second time that you're lying, is it plain to you now on the third time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a conversation between you and me and the people there. I later on checked that out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking the questions. Let's move on because I haven't got enough time. We'll now come to the letter. "Cupina --" and I'm reading the letter, and I'm going to interrupt. I asked you for the letter because this isn't the original letter. Two key things are lacking from the letter, but even a distorted letter of this kind will be sufficient to speak about the actual state of affairs in Mostar. So this letter occurred when you lost the east bank, when you all crossed from the left bank of the river Neretva to the right bank. And I'm now talking about the vast majority of Bosniaks who lived in the eastern part of Mostar, and some of the Croats, because the Serbs had already left. I'm talking about the thousands of Bosniaks who came in from Eastern Herzegovina, and it was general chaos. But this is what I write to you: "I hope that everything passed in the best possible way. I have all information about the situation in Mostar. I recommend as a friend of our peoples, I believed in that then -" that's my comment - "to leave politics alone. And in that case -" and this is what is lacking in the sentence - "your people will leave you too." Mr. Cupina, they came to tell me that they had decided to kill you then. The product of that sentence is that and the letter to try and save your life. That is what I did, out of my convictions and gratitude for having had proper cooperation up until then because I knew your family and because I hoped that you were not guilty. That was my comment. I'm going to continue reading the letter now. "After the war, let the politicians deal with topics that some people on both sides are trying to deal with now." Which two sides am I thinking of when I say that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since you wrote the letter, you interpret it for yourself. I know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Well, I came to The Hague with my letter to explain that to you. I meant the Bosniaks. I was referring to the Bosniaks. And I'm talking to Dzeba now. "I'm quite clear on the position you find yourselves in." Dzeba was the commander of the military police in Mostar, by the way. "It is not essential who is in command. The important thing is that we're not killed by the Chetniks and that the town -- they don't take the town, take control of the town." Cupina, I was busy saving the town, if you will believe me, at that time. Do you believe me or not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't believe you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Thank you. Thank you. I'll continue reading the letter. There's not much more to go. "You should be tolerant and talk to Dzeba and Zelenika and solve all the problems." Were Zelenika and Dzeba the most responsible people in the HVO of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you. New sentence: "Unfortunately, it seems that some people among you do not understand who is stronger, who has more weapons, food, support, and the desire to fight for a free Mostar. Your people know that." And my comment is, and I should like to convince you of that, is that the vast majority of your people knew that too. If you don't know as the commander of that people, I thought you were the real commander. That was comment. And now a distorted sentence which reads as follows: "You can expect no good, you or your people." The comment is: This isn't a threat as it appears here. It was a message, a well-intentioned message which confirms -- which is confirmed by the very next sentence: "This letter is a friendly letter and an unofficial one, and you can't refer to it. I hope that things will improve. Yours, Valentin." The quotation from the book is your comment. After that letter, you say: "This letter, too, from Valentin Coric was a political attempt in the difficult military and political circumstances to exert psychological pressure and political pressure upon me." I won't read any further. Mr. Cupina, after that, I have a few more short questions. I think that they're highly significant. I would need hours to ask them, but I think it would be a good thing for this trial, Your Honours, for the following reason, if I were to ask them: We come to the root of the tragedy in Mostar here. I should like to mention this can be seen from the following question: Mr. Cupina, do you remember that I suggested when I came as the number one man of the military police of the HVO that we establish a military police in Mostar, a joint military police in Mostar, in which the ratio would be 50/50, 50 Croats -- 50 per cent Croats and 50 per cent Bosniaks. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the conflict and clash arose over who was going to head that police force? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you that I put forth Zeljko Dzidic for the commander, because the police in Mostar already existed. Do you remember that or not? In the war with the Serbs, there was a commander sitting behind me now, and I'm sure you are aware of that, if you're honest. When Mostar was liberated from the Serbo-Chetniks, you will -- do you remember which units crossed the Neretva first? Quite literally waded through or swam across the river Neretva?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what position along the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the name Zeljko Dzidic and the military police? Have you heard of Karlo Dzeba?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karlo Dzeba was part of the Independent Battalion at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Well, ask Karlo Dzeba who he crossed the Neretva with.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, I will. But Karlo Dzeba was part of the Independent Battalion, the Cernica Company. He was a very honest and courageous fighter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Karlo Dzeba, after your departure from the Independent Battalion, was a permanent member of the HVO and in recent years he was my assistant in MUP in the Herzegovina-Neretva canton?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I have hundreds of questions to ask you. Mr. Cupina, when you wrote your book, did you use the indictment from The Hague Tribunal against Prlic et al.?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason for that. I know the situation very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Yes or no, please. I would now like to read out for Their Honours something from page 482 of your book. I haven't asked you anything yet. Please let me continue. On page 482, the title is "Criminal activities of the HVO." And there's a footnote, 83, footnote 83, and I'm going to read out what it says: "In addition to the relevant documentation from the archives of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the indictment was used which the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia raised against Jadranko Prlic and all of us here." Your Honours, those of us who have the book, I have quoted the page, page 482. You can read it. And during your testimony today, you clearly confirm, when asked by someone, that you did use the indictment. Now, why am I asking you that? I'm asking you because yesterday you gave us a monologue about the criminal activities of the HVO. You delivered that monologue yesterday, and you said roughly the following: The HVO killed, raped, destroyed religious sites and buildings, destroyed bridges and everything else. Is that what you said here in court yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably said that in that context, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, as somebody once said, that you learnt that quotation off by heart or, rather, was that book written on the basis of our indictment in part? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to elaborate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: There's no elaboration, just yes or no. I don't have enough time. If the Court gives me enough time, then --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as to the bridges, it's common knowledge who did what.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that, although you deal with the issue in your book. You said who did that. Now, when we're on the subject of bridges, who destroyed the bridges in Mostar? Go on, tell us. And when were they destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I elaborate on that in my book, in the Samurai journal, I said --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you that, Mr. Cupina. What I asked you was this: When and who destroyed the bridges in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Coric. Mr. Cupina, the question that Mr. Coric is asking you is a very simple one: Did you use the indictment in writing your book? So the answer is either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In part, yes. Because of terminology, to use the right expressions and that kind of thing. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I would just like to finish with the topic of bridges. The numerous lies that I heard uttered yesterday and today, I'm just going to read out one sentence: "The main destroyers of the bridges on the river Neretva, pursuant to orders of the HDZ, the Croatian army, the HVO and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, was Valentin Coric." And on the following pages, anybody who takes up this book and looks through it, Mr. Cupina, explains that every bridge was destroyed and who destroyed it. And no mention is made, as far as I know, of the name of Valentin Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] That's what I wanted to ask. Thank you for your patience and thank you, Mr. Cupina, and bon voyage to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President -- Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cupina, Mr. Coric said that in your book you said that he was the person responsible for the destruction of the bridges, and then in other parts of the book in which it appears, according to what Mr. Coric says, that this is no longer claimed. So what do you say about that? Why did you accuse him of such acts in the book whereas in other paragraphs you say that he in fact wasn't responsible for this destruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the magazine Samurai, which is a sports magazine which is published in Croatia, in an interview with Mr. Coric he says that he was responsible for the bridges, the roads, et cetera. And since I know that he was the technical director of the bauxite mine and he had access to industrial explosives, and since I know that he boasted about having his engineer units, his own engineer units, and that the HVO was responsible for some of the bridges. Naturally this magazine exists, this interview exists, and that's what he stated. That's how I can interpret this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric. Let's try and deal with this briefly and rapidly. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I will try to. In his book, Mr. Cupina refers to my interview in Zagreb. Mr. Cupina doesn't know what it means to blow up or to clear off mines, and that's not his profession so I'm not surprised, although he was a high-ranking military commander. So he doesn't know what to mine and demine means. In the region where I was in Herzegovina before the conflict broke out, we mined an area. We planted some explosives under some bridges, some tunnels in the Neretva valley, some parts of the water supply in the area of Western Herzegovina. So we did lay some explosives, some mines as a preparatory measure. If the aggressor used tanks to head in our direction, we would have ignited this. We would have used the explosives. Fortunately, this was not necessary, so we did not destroy anything. To destroy something is one thing, to mine something is another thing, to demine something is yet another thing. Thank you, Mr. Cupina. I hope you have understood this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cupina, what is your response to what the accused has said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by what I said. They acted in this way and they blew things up, because the first bridge in the direction of Jablanica was blown up, and then the bridge at Bijela was blown up, et cetera. And this was done as the aggressor exerted pressure. I'm not saying that the HVO blew up all the bridges, but we know more or less which ones were blown up by the HVO and which ones by the Serbo-Chetniks. The Orthodox church was also blown up by the HVO, and there's video footage of this which I provided to the state security, because it's impossible for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we're talking about bridges for the moment. There's a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, you're a witness for the Chamber, not just for the Bench -- not just for the Prosecution now, and we want to establish the truth. We would like to know if there is a link between the accused Coric and the charges against him, the destruction that you have referred to. Unfortunately, I haven't read your book. I don't know what the contents of your book is and I think that is also the case for the other Judges on the Bench, but in support of your accusations in the book, you say you used to a certain extent the Prosecution's indictment. You wanted to use the indictment for the sake of legal terminology. But you also say that you based your book on the interview that the accused gave with regard to his military knowledge about mining, demining of bridges and of public buildings. So my question is as follows: Apart from the indictment from which you obtained the relevant legal terminology and the interview or the interviews that the accused gave with regard to his military knowledge, did you use any other sources that allowed you to establish the responsibility of the accused Coric with regard to the destruction that you referred to in your book or was this not the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had knowledge, information I obtained on a private basis from people, from soldiers. I supported this information by referring to the Samurai magazine. I'm not saying that only he acted in this way. The HVO acted in this way. He participated, but he accused himself in the Samurai magazine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We don't have much time left. Are there any other members of the Defence who would like to conduct cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There are, Your Honour, and there is no way that we can finish in any considerable time. I have about 15 or 20 minutes. I could probably do 15. As I understand, Ms. Alaburic has about 20 minutes, and Mr. Kovacic has about 15 or 20 minutes. So there's -- I don't see how we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, how much time has Defence counsel taken up in total so far, since at the beginning of the hearing it was quite clear we were supposed to adjourn at 5.15. Since we were 15 minutes late, we've worked until 5.30 p.m., so we should really be concluding now. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour. That's true. However, we must keep in mind that the witness has not been terribly responsive. I for one would move that that his entire testimony be stricken from the record. That would be my preference, not to go any further, just send the gentleman home and strike the entire testimony from the record. I know my colleagues feel the same way. But just picking up on the last issue, perhaps he can ask us -- he can tell us how it is that other witnesses said the bridges were destroyed in 1992 by the Serbs. The gentleman has been confabulating. He's been uncontrollable, both on direct and cross-examination, and I think that was one of the reasons why we're running over time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just a minute. We will give you ten minutes each for your cross-examination. Mr. Karnavas, you have ten minutes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Alaburic is going to go next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cupina, my name is Vesna Alaburic. I'm a lawyer from Zagreb, and I represent General Milivoj Petkovic, whom you didn't mention in your statement nor did you mention him in your testimony yesterday or today apart from the fact that you said that he was a co-signatory of a peace agreement with Sefer Halilovic. So I have very few questions for you in fact. I'd like to clarify certain circumstances. Today and yesterday you said that the only meeting that concerned an exchange of prisoners that you attended and that was held with representatives of the HVO was on the 25th of May, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell us, how is it that you haven't described those other meetings in your report? In your report you only mentioned the meeting of the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably because they weren't very effective. There was nothing to write about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So can you then tell us when these other meetings were held?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I mentioned this in the report but all of this happened a long time ago so I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we then agree that what you have claimed so far is incorrect? You said that the only meeting that you attended that concerned this subject was on the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that was one of the meetings where such matters were discussed where the principle of all for all was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. So Mr. Pusic's Defence showed you a document today, 6D 0006. That's a document dated the 28th of May, 1993. You signed the document, and this document establishes a commission responsible for releasing prisoners -- missing prisoners and civilians and for exchanging them. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If this commission was established on the 28th of May, in that case on whose behalf did you attend a meeting three days earlier on the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's something you can find in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's forget about the report and that record. It mentions a negotiating team of the ABiH and the HVO. I'm referring to the commission now. Can you explain this? If not, just say so. The commission was established on the 28th of May, 1993, and you attended a meeting as a member of the commission, a meeting that was held three days earlier. If you can't explain that, we can move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained that in my report, but people change. The composition of these bodies changed. I said there were more people than that number mentioned in the commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I conclude that you can't say on whose behalf you attended the meeting on the 25th of May since the commission was established on the 28th of May and not before. My following question is: According to your information, Mr. Cupina, this commission established on the 28th of May, was it the first ABiH commission that cooperated with the HVO in respect of releasing and exchanging prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Before this commission was established, was there some other commission in existence or is this the first one?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all about the exchanges of prisoners up until the 25th of May when you attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about exchange of prisoners after the 21st of June, 1993, which is the last day that your report refers to?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With that report, I wrapped up all my activities. I provided the report to the superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about that. You mentioned an agreement of my -- between my client Petkovic and the ABiH commander, Sefer Halilovic. This agreement can be shown to you if necessary. The Prosecutor showed it to you. P 002344 is the number of the document. I assume that you remember it and that it's not necessary for us to show it to you again on the screen. Would you agree with me that this agreement concerns the entire area under HVO and ABiH control?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as you can remember, did that agreement cover a number of subjects? For example, freedom of movement, deployment of UNPROFOR, withdrawal of armed forces, and other subjects?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, it covered all those subjects, all those areas, but I didn't attend that meeting so I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But you can remember the contents of the agreement. Would you agree with me if I said that this agreement was implemented in the zones of responsibility of various corps of the ABiH or, rather, in the operative zones of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about the zone of responsibility that I was in. I don't know anything about the other zones.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did Sefer Halilovic participate in the work of your commission?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did he participate in any capacity in the work of your commission?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't. He was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I thank you. I do apologise. Could we show the witness the following document: P 002512. It's a Prosecution exhibit. This is Prosecution Exhibit P 002512. Could we have a look at the midsection of the document. Could we scroll down a bit, please. Thank you. Mr. Cupina, I'm only interested in the first line under item 2, the liberation, the release of all civilians who for security reasons are in shelters and buildings, in areas where there is combat activity. Please answer the following question: Would you agree with me if I said that certain individuals were placed in shelters and other buildings for security reasons, as stated in this record of the meeting of the negotiations team?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they -- the two sides managed to reach this agreement. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is this what happened? You've signed this. I'd like to remind you of the fact.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what was agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the document that you were shown by the Prosecution - and I'd like to show this document to the witness - the document is P 00619.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To avoid confusion, you mentioned the civilians who were placed in shelters, et cetera, for various reasons. I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that there is a paragraph 1 which also mentions civilians who were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is an objection to me, I know what it says under item 1, but I wanted to clarify what is stated under item 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but when a question is put to the witness, it's necessary to present a full question to the witness, to deal with all the aspects of the question and not just with one aspect, so that in the transcript we now see just that civilians were placed in shelters for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this document hasn't been shown to the witness for the first time but certain parts of this agreement have already been discussed, I thought that it was only necessary to refer to one of the items, namely that there were civilians who had been placed in certain buildings for security reasons. As for the civilians who were in prisons, I thought that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the document that has been shown to you by the Prosecution, P 00619, is a document -- so as not to waste any time, it is an analysis of the actual state of government in the municipality of Mostar, and Mr. Cupina, you said that you participated in drafting this document, in a certain sense, because the person who is the author of the document came to your flat, you discussed this document, and on page number 3, in the middle of page number 3 -- could we see the B/C/S version of the text, please or, rather, could we see the Bosniak version. P 01619. That is not it. This is the document analysis of the current situation, government situation, in the municipality of Mostar. I presume that Mr. Cupina will recall this part: On -- in the middle of the second page it is stated that the Bosniak people as the majority people in B and H are committed to a sovereign and undivided Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Cupina, I should like to know what this adjective "undivided" means for you. Does it presuppose a unitary set-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina without any territorial entities which would claim some sort of autonomy or have the characteristics of a republic or something else?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina within its AVNOJ boundaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Actually, Ms. Alaburic, I am very sorry for that, but I have to remind you that you have used more than -- about 12 minutes. So although the Bench was of course very flexible when we decided to give you, each of you, ten more minutes, but also in view of the interpreters, et cetera, I would kindly ask you to finish now and to give the time also to -- other counsel as well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Your Honour. I shall not be asking any further questions, but may I just ask the record to state what it was that I wanted to ask about. I wished to place -- put a question about the distinction of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an undivided, i.e., composite, complex state, a state which would have states within a state within its AVNOJ borders. I also wanted to ask questions about documents signed by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and according to which the HVO is an equally legal military force as the army of the B and H, and I also wanted to ask questions about the alleged military putsch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cupina, with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina undivided.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This refers to -- just to Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in accordance with the legal -- with the constitution and the valid laws. The republic within AVNOJ borders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I have to say that I will cede my time to my colleague simply because of the fact that the -- that the witness never referred directly to my client in his statement, but I should like to ask the Court also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I think that the -- this witness has today committed the offence, the criminal offence of perjury and that his testimony should be viewed from that standpoint and adequate measures taken and not simply just not attribute adequate weight to his statement. I believe it is quite evident that the witness simply does not know some things and when he does know some things he just refrains from stating his knowledge, and that is perjury in my book. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Cupina, you gave a statement back in January, 2004; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was after that you gave your statement that you published your book; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So your book came after your interview; right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were you preparing your book at the time that you gave the statement or was it after you gave the statement that you began writing your book?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to journalists. I gave an interview to the Vecernje Novine in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you here. My question was very precise. Now, you claim to be a university graduate -- claim. So tell me: Did you begin to write the book after you gave the statement? It's "yes," "no," "I don't know," "I can't remember," "maybe"; any of the five.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I gave statements to the effect that I was writing a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you gave the statement, sir, back in January, 2004, had you already begun writing your book or did you write your book afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had prepared the book. Before that I was waiting for adequate financial conditions to be able to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So let me make sure I understand this clearly: You had written the book prior to giving your statement in 2004, and you were waiting for financial conditions so you could publish this book with your own money. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you would have written the book, then, prior to the indictment; right? Because you make references to the indictment here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say "prepared," you mean prepared intellectually or had you already drafted some pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just put together the events, and I composed it. Actually, what I had at that period was -- in that period was my prepared notes and the compilation of documents. I had everything prepared in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I -- sorry. I must insist to have this quite clear. You had prepared all the material but you had not written the text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text was written in 1993 and 1994, in the columns which were published in the papers, and later on I expanded and amplified on those text in the later years, and I elaborated on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By the way, when you met with the Prosecutors, you didn't inform them about your text, did you? That's a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I noticed that one of the reviewers of the text was mentioned earlier, but just to make sure who is credited, is the mufti, the Mufti Smajkic, who is rather a very vocal person in the Muslim community in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it before coming here you met with the mufti, he of course knowing that you were going to come and testify, since you already had made announcements to that in the press as part of the promotion of your book. Is that a yes or a no? It's a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mufti is a friend of mine, and I meet with him every now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see each other very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you met with him before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was at this promotion in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you met with him -- you met with him before coming here to The Hague, prior to coming to testify. Okay [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I haven't seen him since the promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was it you who contacted the Prosecution or did they contact you in order to give a statement?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, they called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to go -- I want to show you your statement, and I apologise for not having this all ready in the e-court, but I have a -- one copy for you to look at in your language, and I have one for the ELMO, and I believe the number we should give it is 1D 00527. And if we could just put the front page on the ELMO. And, sir, if you could look at it. Look at the front page and then look at the back page and tell us whether you recognise this document and whether that is indeed your signature.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you have the one -- the one that you're looking at, sir, that's in your language; is that correct? The one that's on the ELMO is in English. The one in front of you should be in B/C/S. Do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at page 2, and that would be page 3 in yours. In the English, it would be page -- page 2 for the ELMO, that is. In yours it would be page 3. I would like you to look at paragraphs 7 and 8, and then 8 to 9. If you could just look at them. On paragraph 7 we have the date -- it starts with "From 19 September 1991." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then if you go to paragraph 8, we see 1 April, 1992. Do you see that, sir? Paragraph 8. Just tell me if -- is it -- does it -- okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then we skip to paragraph 9. It says between 9 May and 28 May, 1993. Is that how yours starts as well in B/C/S? Look at your copy, sir. Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. It would be fair to say that there's nothing in between April, 1992, and 9 May, at least if we're looking at this document in a chronological order. You provide no information - zero - to the investigators there, who were there, according to you, contacting you for information about the events that you were participating in from 1991 to 1993 or 1994; correct? Now --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get your question, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now, if you could just go through the pages. Just flip through the pages, sir, and tell me if there's anything for the period between April, 1992, and May, 1993, anywhere that you describe anything that you were involved in. Just -- you can just flip through the pages.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's nothing like that in this document, in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And yet at the time -- at the time when the investigators came, sir, they came to talk to you about those events, right, 1992 to 1993? Correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And they wanted you to tell them everything that you knew of that period. And from what you told us, your memory might have been -- would have been quite fresh because you were preparing your book, hence my earlier questions locking the witness in; correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you go the appropriate paragraph, and I'm just going to deal with Mr. Prlic, although I might touch on Mr. Coric just to be fair to the gentleman, but on Mr. Prlic, if we could go to paragraph 36, I want you to look at that, and if I could have Madam Usher's assistance that would be on page 7. For you, sir, it would be page -- it would be page -- page 11. And I want to focus on this, because today you told us -- you answered the question, the specific question posed to you by the Prosecutor. But first if we look at this paragraph, you talk about Mr. Prlic being in the Alliance for Special Purposes; correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Special Purposes Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then you go on to talk about knowing him through sports to some extent; correct? And that he followed the football club Velez; correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lokomotiva, in fact, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is what you're saying here. And then if you look at the last three lines, he says he was very straight that Mostar should be Croat dominated. "I didn't see him between May and September, 1993. Now I see him as president of the pro-European party. He is here in Sarajevo all the time." That's what you say; correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, there's nothing in the statement as far as what you told us here today - and I'm quoting - I'm going to go to page 37 of today's transcript. You say today that you met him in Siroki Brijeg. Nothing in your statement about seeing him in Siroki Brijeg; correct? Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the record, that was on line 22. Now, if we go to line 24, you say that you had -- in a conversation, he told you that this area would be called Herceg-Bosna. Nothing in your statement there either, is there? Okay.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That there would be -- this is on line 25, page 37, again today's transcript: "There would be a parastate within a state." Nothing in your statement about that; right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "And the HVO were the only representatives in the area." This is on page 28, line 1. Nothing in your statement about that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well if there isn't, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to go step-by-step, sir. I just want to nail this one down. "He said things to the effect that we as Muslims had no claim that we could make." Nothing in your statement about that, is there? There's no sense in -- I'm looking at that paragraph, sir. You can look through the rest of the statement but you won't find it there, will you? Will you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't look through it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't go through the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- report quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 36 you, with all your degrees, is it in there? Is it in paragraph 36? And we'll have -- the court will be provided with the entire document, so in case I'm lying, they'll catch me. Nothing in there where Prlic says to you things to the effect, "We as Muslims have no claim that we could make." Nothing there, sir, is there? Sir, there's nothing in there, is there?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this text, there isn't, no. Not in this text here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you gave your statement when things were fresh in your mind and things were percolating because you were getting ready or you had already started writing your book, okay, you didn't say anything to the effect that Prlic said that "we should go to our enclave. I think he mentioned Zenica, Sarajevo, et cetera." Nothing in your statement about is there, sir? Nothing in your statement about that, is there, sir?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this statement has been compiled in such a way --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I know that that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, listen to me: Is it in your statement? It's a yes or a no, or maybe, maybe the investigator from the Prosecution was so unfair to you or incompetent they just failed to put it in. Which of it is it? Isn't it a fact, sir that you never said any of that to the investigator when they came to see you back in January, 2004? Sir, it's not in your statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that here, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, are you claiming today, sir, that you said it and that the investigator failed to put it in? Is that what you're claiming here today? Because we'll call the investigator.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What, you mean for the series, for the articles, the columns?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, listen to me.

utterances.speaker: SUAD CUPINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I was following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it in your statement? When you were questioned by the investigator, did you say any of the lies that you told us here today under oath that Prlic said to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I'm going to object. Going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- beyond that, Your Honour, I've tried to let this go on and give a wide latitude --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, is it in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The witness says in paragraph 36, just in fairness, in fairness to the witness: "I had several contacts with Prlic on issues in Mostar." "I had several contacts on issues in Mostar." This was during 1992, by the way, 1992, not just 1993, and 1993. "We knew each other and were talking about different political views. He was very straight that Mostar should be Croat dominated." Now, that may be all that the investigator wrote down at the time. Maybe Mr. -- maybe Mr. Karnavas wants to take issue with the investigator who prepared this statement, but I do not think it's -- it's fair to make these kind of categorical assertions against the witness based on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hence our letter yesterday -- hence our letter yesterday, Your Honour. When you send an investigator out there and you don't take a tape-recorded statement, you see, we're having it both ways. Now they're claiming that the witness said these things --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- and the investigator failed to put it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- Mr. Karnavas knows that it is not the standard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your question? What question do you wish to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Whether any of the things that he said here today are in the statement that he gave back in January 20th, 2004, when he claims to have written all this book and had all this knowledge percolating in his head. Is it in his statement? Is it there? Yes or no. That's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cupina, there are a lot of things that were raised during the two days of testimony here. Mr. Prlic's counsel is putting it to you that when you -- on the 20th of January, 2004, you did not tell the investigator about those elements. So what do you have to say to us today? Did you tell the investigator who then failed to record it or did you not say anything like that to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the investigator put all my answers into a single sentence and formulated it in one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you want to say that everything you've been saying here and could have said here over the past two days you told the investigator who summarised it in just a few sentences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's roughly it. We spent days talking. Well, I don't know how many days, but we spent a long time discussing everything. I know that we had a long conversation just as we're having a long -- well, it seems that I'm in the dock now here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to the best of your recollections, you did not hide anything from the investigator or omit anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I don't think I hid anything. I talked and they put it into sentence form. I didn't write the sentences myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we have to wind up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, the gentleman said that he spoke for days. He only spoke for one day to the investigator, so I put to the witness that he's lying right now. That he just committed perjury, because here it's one day, not days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many days did the interview last with the investigator; one day or a number of days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that I contacted them over a period of several days, but on that one day I remember it was a very, very long day for me. We went on for the whole day. Now, how many days I can't really say. They kept calling me up for something, but I can't pinpoint the duration in terms of time, whether they asked me because of the statement or because of our contacts, but I know that I spent a whole long day over there. And they kept calling me up as well. I know that it was very hard on me to contend with all this with all the other business I had to attend to. It was very difficult for me to concentrate and focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have one other area, Your Honour. I'll skip through most of the other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were shown a document earlier, a document that was generated by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you ask the question, we have seven more minutes on the tape, and we have to finish in five minutes to replace the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying. I'm trying. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to go back to a document that was brought up by the Prosecution and it was referenced by Ms. Nozica. It's P 1530. This was a document generated back in 1993. If we could pull it up on the -- on the e-court. But just -- and while this is being done, this was a document and you were shown paragraph 2. In this particular paragraph and further on, you're being accused of being a collaborator with the HVO security and information service; is that correct?
